report.body:
A Civil Police investigation in Água Clara ended with five men arrested and
about 54.64 kilograms of drugs seized. The arrests occurred on the night of
Wednesday 4 November 2026 after an anonymous tip said a Volkswagen Gol was being
used to sell drugs. Military Police received information that a man was
selling drugs from a white VW Gol in the Jardim das Palmeiras neighbourhood. When officers approached, the driver tried to flee and was caught after a
pursuit of a few blocks. A portion of a substance resembling cocaine was
found in the car.

At the 30-year-old driver's home, officers seized portions of cannabis, a
precision scale, drug-packaging material and money. The driver was already
a target of the Civil Police's General Investigations Section (SIG) and was
arrested in flagrante. A task force of Military and Civil Police officers
also found two people involved at a snack bar. Information from the
operation led the teams to a drug hideout in a wooded area near the MS-324 road. At the stash, officers found 59 tablets of cannabis weighing about 54
kilograms and arrested two men, aged 18 and 20, in flagrante. A fourth
suspect, aged 22, was arrested with about 500 grams of cannabis and a precision
scale. A fifth man, aged 28, already investigated for drug trafficking and
holding an open arrest warrant, was also found and arrested. A bag holding
19 portions of cocaine totalling about 120 grams, which the first suspect was
said to have dropped during the Military Police approach, was also found.

The Civil Police put the operation's tally at about 54.64 kilograms of drugs,
cannabis and cocaine together, plus a car, a motorcycle, three precision scales,
three mobile phones, drug packaging and about 250 reais in cash. Four of
the five men were booked in flagrante for drug trafficking and association for
trafficking, and the fifth was captured under a court order. Those involved
were taken to the Água Clara Civil Police station for the legal steps. The
operation was carried out jointly by the Civil Police and the Military Police.

worker to six years of aggravated imprisonment for possessing hashish with

panel chaired by Counselor Wagih Hamza Shaqweer, with members Counselors Yasser

the Badr police district, intending to traffic it and outside the circumstances
permitted by law.

A Badr police station investigations officer testified that, posted at a
security checkpoint in the district, he saw the accused showing signs of
suspicion and asked to search her belongings, which she allowed. He found
125 brown pieces of hashish, a cannabis resin, in her belongings, together with
a sum of money and a mobile phone. The 125 pieces weighed 9 kilograms and
350 grams in all, and the chemical laboratory confirmed that the samples
examined from them were hashish listed in the schedules of the anti-drug law.

According to the officer, the accused admitted holding the drugs for
trafficking, said the money found with her came from her dealing, and used the
mobile phone to contact customers.

report.body:
On 1 October 2026, detectives of the Mossos d'Esquadra criminal investigation
division (DIC) arrested seven men, aged 29 to 55, allegedly tied to an
organisation dedicated to drug trafficking. The raid took place at an
industrial warehouse in Cabanes (Girona) and seized 8,025 kilograms of hashish. Officers who entered the building found the seven men unloading pallets
from a trailer, intending to move the hashish into vans for later distribution. The drug was hidden in large raffia sacks filled with rubber crumb, a
system used to hinder its detection at police or customs checks.

The case began in June 2026, when Mossos stopped a van in Viladecans (Barcelona)
carrying about 2,400 kilograms of hashish. Agents later determined that the
drug in the van came from the industrial warehouse in Cabanes. The drug
squad of the DIC in Sant Feliu de Llobregat identified the site as used solely
to store and distribute narcotics. Surveillance of the site recorded people
and vehicles coming and going with no business activity. At the start of
October, officers watched repeated movements of people and vans and the arrival
of an articulated lorry. Several people swapped the vehicles' original
licence plates for others fixed with zip ties, apparently to hinder
identification. Investigators, with the support of the ARRO of Girona, then
entered the premises. A firearm was found in one of the detainees' vans
during the search.

The seven detainees were brought before the Civil and Instruction Section of the
Tribunal de Instancia, a first-instance court, in Figueres. The news site
ElCaso reported that four of the seven were remanded in provisional prison
without bail and the other three also entered prison, with bail. Police
valued the seizure at more than 16.2 million euros on the illicit market.
Police figures cited by La Razón put the 8 tonnes at more than half, 53.9%, of
the 14.9 tonnes of hashish the Mossos had seized in 2026 to date, placing the
operation among the force's most significant. The investigation remains
open and further arrests are not ruled out.

report.title: Driver remanded in custody over 300 kg hashish found in Ceuta port truck
report.summary: Spain's UDYCO drug unit arrested a truck driver at the port of Ceuta after a drugs dog alerted to hashish bags hidden in a double floor, with estimates of the haul around 300 kilograms pending an official weighing. On 15 November 2026 the judicial authority remanded him in custody for an offence against public health, and the investigation remains open.
report.body:
Spain's UDYCO drug unit arrested a truck driver at the port of Ceuta carrying a
stash of hashish hidden in a sophisticated false bottom. The double floor was fitted at the rear of the cab and at the end of the cargo area of the truck. The arrest took place on Friday 13 November 2026. Officers
intercepted the truck on the port road at the Muelle de Poniente and searched it
with support from the UPR prevention unit and the canine group. They found
the hashish and detained the driver, showing him the drugs found in the vehicle
he was driving.

The truck appeared empty and was heading toward boarding for Spain when a
specialist drugs dog alerted, prompting an exhaustive hours-long search inside
and outside the vehicle. Officers used hammers, cutters, sledgehammers and an angle grinder to break open the metal sheeting that hid the double floor. After the hours-long detailed inspection, officers
found a large number of bags full of hashish inside the truck's structure.
Officers recovered numerous bags of hashish from the trailer's false bottom,
with first estimates putting the haul above 300 kilograms although police gave
no official weight. The submitted account describes the seizure as about
300 kilograms of hashish arriving from Morocco.

The handcuffed driver was taken to police headquarters and placed under
investigation for an offence against public health. On Sunday 15 November 2026 the driver was placed at the disposal of the judicial authority, which remanded him in custody for an offence against public health. Police link the
operation to open UDYCO investigations into groups moving hashish from Ceuta to
mainland Spain in heavy vehicles with hidden compartments.

report.body:
National Police in Palma arrested four men and a woman who allegedly belonged to
a group dedicated to drug trafficking, seizing 60 kilograms of hashish and
weapons. The Grupo I de Estupefacientes of the National Police closed an
investigation begun months earlier that ended with the five arrests, the force
said in a statement.

Officers learned of a hashish package addressed to a man living in Palma,
identified him, seized the package, which contained 24 kilograms of hashish, and
arrested him for a possible drug trafficking offence. Investigators then
established that further suspects were collaborating and that two homes could
hold more substances, and officers searched both. In the first home, that
of the main suspect, officers found 36 kilograms of hashish, an air rifle with a
silencer and about 10,000 euros in cash. The man and a woman were arrested
there as the suspected authors of drug trafficking and membership of a criminal
group or organisation.

In the second home, officers arrested a suspect who allegedly guarded and
transported drugs. That home held two kilograms of cocaine, doses of the
drug, cutting agent, a nine-millimetre pistol with cartridges, a bow with arrows
and a hydraulic press allegedly used to compress the cocaine, which is not
counted in the cannabis figures. A further person was arrested in
connection with the case. The five detainees are accused of drug
trafficking and membership of a criminal organisation. Police suspect the
drugs were being distributed to third parties for smaller-scale sale, and the
investigation remains open with further arrests not ruled out. Agents of
the Unidad de Prevención y Reacción, the Grupo II de Estupefacientes and the
police dog handler unit also took part in the searches.

report.body:
A Ukrainian driver was arrested at Saint-Lary-Soulan, in the Hautes-Pyrénées, on
28 September 2026 while transporting more than 32 kilograms of herbal cannabis. The Renault Talisman, driven by a Ukrainian man living in Poland with no
criminal record, was stopped at 22:15 as it returned from Spain through the
Aragnouet-Bielsa tunnel. A customs administrator said the Aragnouet tunnel,
like the central Pyrenees, is a route increasingly used by criminal networks. Under a carpet that was not original, the officers found two metal caissons
holding 32 heat-sealed bags of herbal cannabis, 32.8 kg in all. The goods
were valued at 131,200 euros, and rags soaked in white spirit had been placed in
the car to mask the smell of the drug.

The driver told the court he had been recruited through Telegram and paid 3,000
euros to carry the goods from Alicante, in Spain, to Poland. Tried under
the comparution immédiate, France's immediate-appearance procedure, the young
father of a son a few weeks old did not conceal his role when caught in
flagrante delicto. He was tried by the Tarbes criminal court on 1 October
2026. The tribunal sentenced him to 24 months' imprisonment and a ten-year
ban from French territory (interdiction du territoire français). The prison
term takes effect under a committal order, and a conditional release with
expulsion was proposed to him as a sentence adjustment.

The customs side of the judgment imposed a 131,200-euro fine for transporting
narcotics without the required supporting document and 405 euros for customs
money laundering, 131,605 euros in all. The court also confiscated the 32.8
kg of cannabis, 405 euros in banknotes, two telephones and a computer. The
judge told him he could "be more useful to his country on his return" than by
practising smuggling in France.

in banknotes, and two telephones and a computer. The customs service said
the operation showed the importance of its controls on transport moving through

exercise at Yaruni Bend, Linden, in the Upper Demerara River area, between 5:30

narcotics destroyed at $22,038,728, covering the plants and the dried cannabis. No arrests were made, and investigations are continuing.

The Criminal Investigation Department of the Ajdabiya Security Directorate
raided a residential flat in the city of Ajdabiya and seized narcotics, tramadol
pills and a sum of money, the directorate's security media unit reported.

from private sources that a quantity of drugs and hallucination pills was stored
in a flat on the third floor of a residential building in the city, with an
intention to move the seizures to another hiding place to conceal a dealing
operation. Officers took the necessary legal measures, opened an inquiry
record and notified the public prosecution, which issued its authorisation to
raid the flat and seize the offenders.

hashish, 59 boxes of the painkiller tramadol totalling 5,529 tablets, and 16,500
Libyan dinars in cash. The seizures were hidden inside a bag designed for
carrying children, in an attempt to keep them out of sight.

After the information was verified, a security force stormed the flat and
arrested suspects, whose number was not specified; they confessed during
investigations to what was attributed to them and were referred to the public
prosecution. Officers secured the drugs and the money and took the suspects
to the station to complete the inquiry procedures. The security media unit
said the operation was part of security efforts to combat drugs and psychotropic
substances and to pursue those involved in possessing and distributing them.

Saudi Arabia executed three Ethiopian nationals in the Asir region on Wednesday
7 October 2026. The Interior Ministry named the executed men as Seni Redi
Aqous Qorzqor, Shanafi Tekay Anbayeh Barah and Mersu Negus Akalu Tele. The
three were convicted of jointly smuggling hashish into the Kingdom.

Security authorities apprehended the three, and investigations led to charges
before the competent court. The court confirmed the charges and sentenced
the three to death as a discretionary punishment. The ruling was upheld on
appeal and confirmed by the Supreme Court, and a royal order was issued to carry
out the sentence in accordance with Islamic law.

The Interior Ministry said the announcement affirms the government's commitment
to protecting citizens and residents from drugs and to imposing the strictest
penalties prescribed by law on traffickers and dealers. Human Rights Watch
said on the day of the execution that at least 17 Ethiopian nationals had been
executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 without due process, with dozens more at
imminent risk of execution over drug-related offences. The group had
reported in July that Ethiopian migrants were being executed after court
hearings that sometimes lasted only a few minutes, without a lawyer or a
translator, and that at least 79 more Ethiopians faced imminent execution on
similar charges.

report.body:
Thai immigration police raided a rented luxury house on Soi Khu Bon 27 in Tha
Raeng, Bang Khen district, Bangkok, on 19 October 2026, under a Min Buri
Criminal Court search warrant. The search was carried out by the
Immigration Bureau's special operations unit with officials from the Department
of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine, on the orders of the national
police chief. The raid followed complaints from nearby residents about a
strong, lingering smell of cannabis. Officers spent about two months
gathering evidence before raiding the house, a three-storey detached property of
about 100 square wah in a housing estate. The house had an installed
ventilation system designed to expel the cannabis smell outside. Police
found cannabis buds weighing over five tonnes, packed in black bags hidden
throughout all three floors of the house.

Officers arrested a Vietnamese man and four Myanmar employees after finding five
tonnes of cannabis buds on the premises. The Myanmar workers were paid 200
to 300 baht a day to sort and pack the buds. Authorities believe the
Vietnamese suspect was overseeing the operations, which appeared to be managed
like a company. A Thai individual had signed the lease agreement before the
foreigners moved in and operated the site for over a year. The house was
used as a base for storing, sorting and packaging cannabis buds before
distribution to customers. The suspects remained in custody as authorities
pursued further investigation and legal action.

The group held a licence for cannabis bud processing in Nong Bua Lam Phu
province, but their business in Bangkok was illegal. Under the 1999 Thai
Traditional Medical Act, anyone wishing to sell, process or export cannabis buds
must obtain a licence valid for the specific area. The offence carries a
maximum penalty of one year in prison, a fine of up to 20,000 baht, or both. The seized cannabis buds will be sent to a laboratory for testing to
determine whether they were locally grown or imported. Police were working
to track down the Thai national who originally rented the property. Police
were expanding the investigation, saying nationals of Myanmar, Vietnam and China
were involved in the case.

Immigration police and officials of the Department of Thai Traditional and
Alternative Medicine raided a rented three-storey luxury home in Bangkok's Bang
Khen district under a search warrant issued by the Min Buri Criminal Court.
The raid took place on Monday, 19 October 2026. Officers arrested one
Vietnamese national and four Myanmar nationals who were sorting cannabis flowers
for packaging and distribution to customers across Bangkok. Black trash
bags stuffed with cannabis buds were scattered across all three floors of the
house. The total seizure weighed more than five tonnes (over 5,000
kilograms). The four Myanmar workers were reportedly paid 200 to 300 baht
per day. Police suspect the Vietnamese national supervised the daily
operations.

Neighbours endured the heavy scent for weeks before alerting the local
authorities, and officers spent two full months investigating the property
before moving in. The house was fitted with a custom exhaust pipe system to
try to hide the heavy scent. A Thai person had rented the property before
the foreign nationals moved in, and the site had reportedly been used to store,
sort and package cannabis for more than a year.

The operators held a licence that was valid only for Nong Bua Lamphu province,
not Bangkok. Onanong Srisuwan, a legal officer from the Department of Thai
Traditional and Alternative Medicine, said processing and selling cannabis
requires a strict local permit. Under the Thai Traditional Medical
Knowledge Protection and Promotion Act, violators can face up to one year in
prison or a fine of up to 20,000 baht. Police are sending the seized
cannabis for laboratory testing to determine whether it was grown in Thailand or
imported. Investigators are also tracing the Thai tenant, the source of the
cannabis and any financiers involved.

A court in Mykolaiv has convicted a 51-year-old local man of illegally making
and storing narcotics for sale in especially large amounts and of illegally
sowing and growing cannabis. The Ingulskyi District Court of Mykolaiv
sentenced him to nine years in prison for growing cannabis on his homestead plot
and keeping the dried, shredded drug in the attic of his house. The verdict
has not entered into legal force. It may be appealed to the Mykolaiv Appeal
Court within 30 days of its pronouncement.

Officers of Police Station No. 2 of the Mykolaiv District Police Department
uncovered the case in July 2026. The prosecution put the cannabis kept in
the attic at more than 8 kilograms. Police described the seizure as more
than 10 kilograms of dried narcotic raw material, together with the 14 cannabis
plants.

The court established that the man had grown the cannabis on the territory of
his household since April 2026. He tended the plants carefully, fertilising
the soil, clearing the plot of weeds and watering them regularly. He dried
part of the harvest in the attic and had already shredded the rest into glass
jars for storage and, according to investigators, for sale. He was detained
in procedural order and informed of the suspicion of illegal production,
manufacture, acquisition, storage for sale and sale of narcotics in especially
large amounts, and of sowing or cultivating soporific poppy or cannabis. At
the time of the detention police said the charges carried up to 12 years in
prison with confiscation of property. A court placed the suspect in custody
with the possibility of posting more than 133,000 hryvnias in bail. The
bail was set at 133,120 hryvnias, which the man's brother paid by taking out a
loan.

In court the man partially admitted his guilt: he conceded that he grew the
cannabis and made the drug from it, but insisted he had done so only for his own
use, not for sale. The court rejected the claim, reading his statement that
he had kept such a quantity for personal use as an attempt to avoid criminal
liability. It also took into account that the man had previously served a
five-year prison term for growing cannabis. The court ordered the seized
plants and cannabis destroyed and recovered 28,400 hryvnias in

attempts.decision_title: South Africa legalisation routed to CFI history
attempts.explanation: The Al Jazeera feature reports that President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Cannabis for Private Purposes Act just before South Africa's general election, removing cannabis from the country's list of outlawed narcotics and making South Africa the first African nation to legalise recreational use. This is a change in the law and in the country's score, so it belongs in the CFI's South Africa history rather than the tracker, which records enforcement events only. The enforcement the article mentions is passing context - the 2012 Ras Gareth Prince arrest behind the 2017 and 2018 landmark rulings, the 2020 raid on The Haze Club in Johannesburg with legal proceedings continuing, and police helicopters spraying Eastern Cape dagga fields with herbicides - none reported as this article's own event with dates or figures, and tracker searches found no existing report on the Haze Club raid or the Prince case to update. A follow-up source reporting an actual raid, arrest or prosecution under the new act would be a tracker event.
